You have attempted this same task before and did not succeed. These are the plans you wrote after those attempts.
Trial #1: New plan: My previous attempt failed because I tracked the positions of all players, which introduced unnecessary complexity and increased the risk of tracking errors, even though I correctly identified that Bob was only involved in the first and last swaps. The mistake was not in the logic of the specific steps I took, but in the inefficiency of the strategy which made the solution fragile. Next time, I will adopt a "target-focused" strategy: I will identify the specific player the question asks about (Bob) and only track the position of that specific player through the sequence of swaps, completely ignoring the movements of other players unless they directly involve the target. I will explicitly verify the target's position after every single swap mentioned in the text, rather than updating a full state table. This minimizes cognitive load and ensures the final answer is derived directly from the target's trajectory.

New plan: My previous attempt failed because I relied on a "target-focused" strategy that required me to mentally reconstruct the state of a third party (Dave) to resolve the final swap, leading to a logic error in tracing Dave's position. Specifically, I incorrectly assumed Dave held the "center midfielder" position at the end, failing to realize that the "center midfielder" position had moved to Gertrude in step 6, while Dave had moved to the "goalkeeper" position. To fix this, I will switch to a "full-state tracking" strategy. I will explicitly list the current position of *every* player (Alice, Bob, Claire, Dave, Eve, Fred, Gertrude) after each swap. By maintaining a complete state map, I will never need to guess or reconstruct the history of a specific player; I will simply read the current position of the partner involved in the swap directly from the updated list. This eliminates the risk of losing track of intermediate movements.
